sets.title: Trigonometry: Right Triangle Ratios and SOH CAH TOA
sets.description: The six trig ratios as sides of a right triangle, plus solving for a missing side or a missing angle. Includes angle of elevation and angle of depression problems.

cards.front: In a right triangle, sin θ equals which ratio of sides?
cards.back: sin θ = opposite ÷ hypotenuse.

cards.front: In a right triangle, cos θ equals which ratio of sides?
cards.back: cos θ = adjacent ÷ hypotenuse.

cards.front: In a right triangle, tan θ equals which ratio of sides?
cards.back: tan θ = opposite ÷ adjacent.

cards.front: In a right triangle, csc θ equals which ratio of sides?
cards.back: csc θ = hypotenuse ÷ opposite. It is the reciprocal of sine.

cards.front: In a right triangle, sec θ equals which ratio of sides?
cards.back: sec θ = hypotenuse ÷ adjacent. It is the reciprocal of cosine.

cards.front: In a right triangle, cot θ equals which ratio of sides?
cards.back: cot θ = adjacent ÷ opposite. It is the reciprocal of tangent.

cards.front: What does the mnemonic SOH CAH TOA stand for?
cards.back: Sine = Opposite ÷ Hypotenuse, Cosine = Adjacent ÷ Hypotenuse, Tangent = Opposite ÷ Adjacent.

cards.front: Which side of a right triangle is the hypotenuse?
cards.back: The side across from the right angle. It is always the longest side of the triangle.

cards.front: How are the opposite and adjacent legs named?
cards.back: Always relative to the acute angle you are working with. The opposite leg is across from θ, and the adjacent leg touches θ without being the hypotenuse.

cards.front: How do the two acute angles of a right triangle relate?
cards.back: They are complementary and add to 90°, because all three angles total 180° and one of them is already 90°.

cards.front: You know an acute angle and the hypotenuse. How do you find the opposite side?
cards.back: Use sine: opposite = hypotenuse × sin θ.

cards.front: You know an acute angle and the hypotenuse. How do you find the adjacent side?
cards.back: Use cosine: adjacent = hypotenuse × cos θ.

cards.front: You know an acute angle and the adjacent side. How do you find the opposite side?
cards.back: Use tangent: opposite = adjacent × tan θ.

cards.front: You know both legs of a right triangle. How do you find an acute angle?
cards.back: Use the inverse tangent: θ = arctan(opposite ÷ adjacent).

cards.front: You know the opposite side and the hypotenuse. How do you find the angle?
cards.back: Use the inverse sine: θ = arcsin(opposite ÷ hypotenuse).

cards.front: You know the adjacent side and the hypotenuse. How do you find the angle?
cards.back: Use the inverse cosine: θ = arccos(adjacent ÷ hypotenuse).

cards.front: What is an angle of elevation?
cards.back: The angle measured upward from a horizontal line of sight to an object above the observer.

cards.front: What is an angle of depression?
cards.back: The angle measured downward from a horizontal line of sight to an object below the observer.

cards.front: How does an angle of depression compare with the matching angle of elevation?
cards.back: They are equal. The two horizontal lines are parallel and the line of sight cuts across both, making the pair alternate interior angles.

cards.front: A 20 foot ladder leans on a wall at 60° to the ground. How high does it reach?
cards.back: Height = 20 × sin 60° = 20 × sqrt(3)/2, which is about 17.3 feet.

sets.title: Trigonometry: Degree and Radian Measure
sets.description: Converting angles in both directions, arc length, sector area, and angles drawn in standard position. Coterminal angles are covered here too.

cards.front: How do you convert an angle from degrees to radians?
cards.back: Multiply by π/180. Example: 135° × π/180 = 3π/4 radians.

cards.front: How do you convert an angle from radians to degrees?
cards.back: Multiply by 180/π. Example: 5π/6 × 180/π = 150°.

cards.front: How many degrees are in π radians?
cards.back: π radians = 180°. A full circle is 2π radians = 360°, so one radian is about 57.3°.

cards.front: What is one radian?
cards.back: The central angle of a circle that cuts off an arc equal in length to the radius.

cards.front: Convert 45° to radians.
cards.back: 45 × π/180 = π/4 radians.

cards.front: Convert 240° to radians.
cards.back: 240 × π/180 = 4π/3 radians.

cards.front: Convert 300° to radians.
cards.back: 300 × π/180 = 5π/3 radians.

cards.front: Convert 7π/4 radians to degrees.
Convert 2π/3 radians to degrees.
Convert 11π/6 radians to degrees.
State the arc length formula.
cards.back: s = rθ, where r is the radius and θ is the central angle in radians. Convert degrees to radians before using it.

cards.front: A circle of radius 6 has a central angle of π/3. What is the arc length?
cards.back: s = rθ = 6 × π/3 = 2π units, about 6.28 units.

cards.front: State the formula for the area of a circular sector.
cards.back: A = (1/2)r²θ, with θ measured in radians.

cards.front: A sector has radius 4 and central angle π/2. What is its area?
What does it mean for an angle to be in standard position?
cards.back: Its vertex sits at the origin and its initial side lies along the positive x-axis.

cards.front: What are the initial side and the terminal side of an angle?
cards.back: The initial side is where the rotation starts, along the positive x-axis in standard position. The terminal side is where the rotation stops.

cards.front: What do positive and negative angle measures mean?
cards.back: A positive angle rotates counterclockwise from the initial side. A negative angle rotates clockwise.

cards.front: What are coterminal angles?
cards.back: Angles in standard position that share the same terminal side. They differ by whole turns, so 360°n in degrees or 2πn in radians.

cards.front: Find a positive angle coterminal with -60°.
cards.back: -60° + 360° = 300°. Any angle of the form -60° + 360°n also works.

cards.front: Find an angle between 0° and 360° coterminal with 400°.

sets.title: Trigonometry: Unit Circle Sine Values
sets.description: One card per angle for the exact sine values around the full unit circle. Sine is the y-coordinate of the point where the terminal side meets the circle.

cards.front: What is sin 0° (0 radians)?
cards.back: sin 0° = 0. The point (1, 0) has y-coordinate 0.

cards.front: What is sin 30° (π/6)?
cards.back: sin 30° = (1/2). Reference angle 30°, and sine is positive in Quadrant I.

cards.front: What is sin 45° (π/4)?
cards.back: sin 45° = sqrt(2)/2. Reference angle 45°, and sine is positive in Quadrant I.

cards.front: What is sin 60° (π/3)?
cards.back: sin 60° = sqrt(3)/2. Reference angle 60°, and sine is positive in Quadrant I.

cards.front: What is sin 90° (π/2)?
cards.back: sin 90° = 1. The point (0, 1) has y-coordinate 1, the largest value sine ever reaches.

cards.front: What is sin 120° (2π/3)?
cards.back: sin 120° = sqrt(3)/2. Reference angle 60°, and sine is positive in Quadrant II.

cards.front: What is sin 135° (3π/4)?
cards.back: sin 135° = sqrt(2)/2. Reference angle 45°, and sine is positive in Quadrant II.

cards.front: What is sin 150° (5π/6)?
cards.back: sin 150° = (1/2). Reference angle 30°, and sine is positive in Quadrant II.

cards.front: What is sin 180° (π)?
cards.back: sin 180° = 0. The point (-1, 0) has y-coordinate 0.

cards.front: What is sin 210° (7π/6)?
cards.back: sin 210° = -(1/2). Reference angle 30°, and sine is negative in Quadrant III.

cards.front: What is sin 225° (5π/4)?
cards.back: sin 225° = -sqrt(2)/2. Reference angle 45°, and sine is negative in Quadrant III.

cards.front: What is sin 240° (4π/3)?
cards.back: sin 240° = -sqrt(3)/2. Reference angle 60°, and sine is negative in Quadrant III.

cards.front: What is sin 270° (3π/2)?
cards.back: sin 270° = -1. The point (0, -1) has y-coordinate -1, the smallest value sine ever reaches.

cards.front: What is sin 300° (5π/3)?
cards.back: sin 300° = -sqrt(3)/2. Reference angle 60°, and sine is negative in Quadrant IV.

cards.front: What is sin 315° (7π/4)?
cards.back: sin 315° = -sqrt(2)/2. Reference angle 45°, and sine is negative in Quadrant IV.

cards.front: What is sin 330° (11π/6)?
cards.back: sin 330° = -(1/2). Reference angle 30°, and sine is negative in Quadrant IV.

cards.front: What is sin 360° (2π)?
cards.back: sin 360° = 0. A full turn lands back on (1, 0), so the value matches 0°.

sets.title: Trigonometry: Unit Circle Cosine Values
sets.description: One card per angle for the exact cosine values around the full unit circle. Cosine is the x-coordinate of the point where the terminal side meets the circle.

cards.front: What is cos 0° (0 radians)?
cards.back: cos 0° = 1. The point (1, 0) has x-coordinate 1, the largest value cosine ever reaches.

cards.front: What is cos 30° (π/6)?
cards.back: cos 30° = sqrt(3)/2. Reference angle 30°, and cosine is positive in Quadrant I.

cards.front: What is cos 45° (π/4)?
cards.back: cos 45° = sqrt(2)/2. Reference angle 45°, and cosine is positive in Quadrant I.

cards.front: What is cos 60° (π/3)?
cards.back: cos 60° = (1/2). Reference angle 60°, and cosine is positive in Quadrant I.

cards.front: What is cos 90° (π/2)?
cards.back: cos 90° = 0. The point (0, 1) has x-coordinate 0.

cards.front: What is cos 120° (2π/3)?
cards.back: cos 120° = -(1/2). Reference angle 60°, and cosine is negative in Quadrant II.

cards.front: What is cos 135° (3π/4)?
cards.back: cos 135° = -sqrt(2)/2. Reference angle 45°, and cosine is negative in Quadrant II.

cards.front: What is cos 150° (5π/6)?
cards.back: cos 150° = -sqrt(3)/2. Reference angle 30°, and cosine is negative in Quadrant II.

cards.front: What is cos 180° (π)?
cards.back: cos 180° = -1. The point (-1, 0) has x-coordinate -1, the smallest value cosine ever reaches.

cards.front: What is cos 210° (7π/6)?
cards.back: cos 210° = -sqrt(3)/2. Reference angle 30°, and cosine is negative in Quadrant III.

cards.front: What is cos 225° (5π/4)?
cards.back: cos 225° = -sqrt(2)/2. Reference angle 45°, and cosine is negative in Quadrant III.

cards.front: What is cos 240° (4π/3)?
cards.back: cos 240° = -(1/2). Reference angle 60°, and cosine is negative in Quadrant III.

cards.front: What is cos 270° (3π/2)?
cards.back: cos 270° = 0. The point (0, -1) has x-coordinate 0.

cards.front: What is cos 300° (5π/3)?
cards.back: cos 300° = (1/2). Reference angle 60°, and cosine is positive in Quadrant IV.

cards.front: What is cos 315° (7π/4)?
cards.back: cos 315° = sqrt(2)/2. Reference angle 45°, and cosine is positive in Quadrant IV.

cards.front: What is cos 330° (11π/6)?
cards.back: cos 330° = sqrt(3)/2. Reference angle 30°, and cosine is positive in Quadrant IV.

cards.front: What is cos 360° (2π)?
cards.back: cos 360° = 1. A full turn lands back on (1, 0), so the value matches 0°.

sets.title: Trigonometry: Unit Circle Tangent Values
sets.description: One card per angle for the exact tangent values around the full unit circle. Tangent is sine divided by cosine, so it is undefined wherever cosine equals zero.

cards.front: What is tan 0° (0 radians)?
cards.back: tan 0° = 0. It works out as sin 0° ÷ cos 0° = 0 ÷ 1.

cards.front: What is tan 30° (π/6)?
cards.back: tan 30° = sqrt(3)/3. Reference angle 30°, and tangent is positive in Quadrant I.

cards.front: What is tan 45° (π/4)?
cards.back: tan 45° = 1. Reference angle 45°, and tangent is positive in Quadrant I.

cards.front: What is tan 60° (π/3)?
cards.back: tan 60° = sqrt(3). Reference angle 60°, and tangent is positive in Quadrant I.

cards.front: What is tan 90° (π/2)?
cards.back: Undefined, because cos 90° = 0 and you cannot divide by zero. The graph has a vertical asymptote there.

cards.front: What is tan 120° (2π/3)?
cards.back: tan 120° = -sqrt(3). Reference angle 60°, and tangent is negative in Quadrant II.

cards.front: What is tan 135° (3π/4)?
cards.back: tan 135° = -1. Reference angle 45°, and tangent is negative in Quadrant II.

cards.front: What is tan 150° (5π/6)?
cards.back: tan 150° = -sqrt(3)/3. Reference angle 30°, and tangent is negative in Quadrant II.

cards.front: What is tan 180° (π)?
cards.back: tan 180° = 0. It works out as sin 180° ÷ cos 180° = 0 ÷ -1.

cards.front: What is tan 210° (7π/6)?
cards.back: tan 210° = sqrt(3)/3. Reference angle 30°, and tangent is positive in Quadrant III.

cards.front: What is tan 225° (5π/4)?
cards.back: tan 225° = 1. Reference angle 45°, and tangent is positive in Quadrant III.

cards.front: What is tan 240° (4π/3)?
cards.back: tan 240° = sqrt(3). Reference angle 60°, and tangent is positive in Quadrant III.

cards.front: What is tan 270° (3π/2)?
cards.back: Undefined, because cos 270° = 0 and you cannot divide by zero. The graph has a vertical asymptote there.

cards.front: What is tan 300° (5π/3)?
cards.back: tan 300° = -sqrt(3). Reference angle 60°, and tangent is negative in Quadrant IV.

cards.front: What is tan 315° (7π/4)?
cards.back: tan 315° = -1. Reference angle 45°, and tangent is negative in Quadrant IV.

cards.front: What is tan 330° (11π/6)?
cards.back: tan 330° = -sqrt(3)/3. Reference angle 30°, and tangent is negative in Quadrant IV.

cards.front: What is tan 360° (2π)?
cards.back: tan 360° = 0. It works out as sin 360° ÷ cos 360° = 0 ÷ 1, the same value as 0°.

sets.title: Trigonometry: Pythagorean, Reciprocal, and Quotient Identities
sets.description: The three Pythagorean identities, all six reciprocal relationships, and both quotient identities. Each card names the angles where the identity is undefined.

cards.front: State the main Pythagorean identity.
cards.back: sin²θ + cos²θ = 1. It comes from x² + y² = 1 on the unit circle, where x = cos θ and y = sin θ.

cards.front: State the Pythagorean identity that uses tangent and secant.
cards.back: 1 + tan²θ = sec²θ. Divide sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 through by cos²θ to get it.

cards.front: State the Pythagorean identity that uses cotangent and cosecant.
cards.back: 1 + cot²θ = csc²θ. Divide sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 through by sin²θ to get it.

cards.front: Why is sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 true for every angle?
cards.back: Every unit circle point is (cos θ, sin θ) and sits exactly one unit from the origin, so the Pythagorean theorem gives cos²θ + sin²θ = 1.

cards.front: Write csc θ in terms of sin θ.
cards.back: csc θ = 1/sin θ, defined whenever sin θ ≠ 0.

cards.front: Write sec θ in terms of cos θ.
cards.back: sec θ = 1/cos θ, defined whenever cos θ ≠ 0.

cards.front: Write cot θ in terms of tan θ.
cards.back: cot θ = 1/tan θ, defined whenever tan θ exists and tan θ ≠ 0.

cards.front: Write sin θ in terms of csc θ.
cards.back: sin θ = 1/csc θ, defined whenever csc θ exists.

cards.front: Write cos θ in terms of sec θ.
cards.back: cos θ = 1/sec θ, defined whenever sec θ exists.

cards.front: Write tan θ in terms of cot θ.
cards.back: tan θ = 1/cot θ, defined whenever cot θ exists and cot θ ≠ 0.

cards.front: State the quotient identity for tangent.
cards.back: tan θ = sin θ / cos θ, defined whenever cos θ ≠ 0.

cards.front: State the quotient identity for cotangent.
cards.back: cot θ = cos θ / sin θ, defined whenever sin θ ≠ 0.

cards.front: For which angles are tan θ and sec θ undefined?
cards.back: Wherever cos θ = 0, which is θ = π/2 + πn radians, or 90° + 180°n, for any integer n.

cards.front: For which angles are cot θ and csc θ undefined?
cards.back: Wherever sin θ = 0, which is θ = πn radians, or 180°n, for any integer n.

cards.front: Rewrite sin²θ and cos²θ using the main Pythagorean identity.
cards.back: sin²θ = 1 - cos²θ and cos²θ = 1 - sin²θ.

cards.front: Simplify sec²θ - tan²θ.
cards.back: It equals 1, straight from rearranging 1 + tan²θ = sec²θ.

cards.front: Simplify csc²θ - cot²θ.
cards.back: It equals 1, straight from rearranging 1 + cot²θ = csc²θ.

cards.front: Simplify sin θ csc θ.
cards.back: It equals 1, since csc θ = 1/sin θ. The same reasoning gives cos θ sec θ = 1 and tan θ cot θ = 1.

sets.title: Trigonometry: Even, Odd, and Cofunction Identities
sets.description: How the six trig functions respond to a negative angle, the six cofunction pairs, and the common shift identities built on π and 2π.

cards.front: Simplify sin(-θ).
cards.back: sin(-θ) = -sin θ. Sine is an odd function.

cards.front: Simplify cos(-θ).
cards.back: cos(-θ) = cos θ. Cosine is an even function.

cards.front: Simplify tan(-θ).
cards.back: tan(-θ) = -tan θ. Tangent is an odd function.

cards.front: Simplify csc(-θ).
cards.back: csc(-θ) = -csc θ. Cosecant is an odd function, matching sine.

cards.front: Simplify sec(-θ).
cards.back: sec(-θ) = sec θ. Secant is an even function, matching cosine.

cards.front: Simplify cot(-θ).
cards.back: cot(-θ) = -cot θ. Cotangent is an odd function, matching tangent.

cards.front: Which trig functions are even and which are odd?
cards.back: Even: cosine and secant. Odd: sine, cosecant, tangent, and cotangent.

cards.front: State the cofunction identity for sine.
cards.back: sin(90° - θ) = cos θ, written sin(π/2 - θ) = cos θ in radians.

cards.front: State the cofunction identity for cosine.
cards.back: cos(90° - θ) = sin θ, written cos(π/2 - θ) = sin θ in radians.

cards.front: State the cofunction identity for tangent.
cards.back: tan(90° - θ) = cot θ, written tan(π/2 - θ) = cot θ in radians.

cards.front: State the cofunction identity for cotangent.
cards.back: cot(90° - θ) = tan θ, written cot(π/2 - θ) = tan θ in radians.

cards.front: State the cofunction identity for secant.
cards.back: sec(90° - θ) = csc θ, written sec(π/2 - θ) = csc θ in radians.

cards.front: State the cofunction identity for cosecant.
cards.back: csc(90° - θ) = sec θ, written csc(π/2 - θ) = sec θ in radians.

cards.front: Why do the cofunction identities work in a right triangle?
cards.back: The two acute angles add to 90°, so the leg opposite one angle is adjacent to the other. Swapping the angle swaps each ratio with its cofunction.

cards.front: Simplify sin(π - θ).
cards.back: sin(π - θ) = sin θ. The angle lands in Quadrant II with reference angle θ, and sine stays positive there.

cards.front: Simplify cos(π - θ).
cards.back: cos(π - θ) = -cos θ. The angle lands in Quadrant II, where cosine is negative.

cards.front: Simplify tan(π - θ).
cards.back: tan(π - θ) = -tan θ. Tangent is negative in Quadrant II.

cards.front: Simplify sin(π + θ).
cards.back: sin(π + θ) = -sin θ. The angle lands in Quadrant III, where sine is negative.

cards.front: Simplify cos(π + θ).
cards.back: cos(π + θ) = -cos θ. The angle lands in Quadrant III, where cosine is negative.

cards.front: Simplify tan(π + θ).
cards.back: tan(π + θ) = tan θ. Tangent repeats every π radians.

sets.title: Trigonometry: Sum and Difference Formulas
sets.description: The six sum and difference formulas for sine, cosine, and tangent, plus exact values for angles such as 15°, 75°, and 105° built from them.

cards.front: Expand sin(A + B).
cards.back: sin(A + B) = sin A cos B + cos A sin B.

cards.front: Expand sin(A - B).
cards.back: sin(A - B) = sin A cos B - cos A sin B.

cards.front: Expand cos(A + B).
cards.back: cos(A + B) = cos A cos B - sin A sin B. The sign flips from plus on the left to minus on the right.

cards.front: Expand cos(A - B).
cards.back: cos(A - B) = cos A cos B + sin A sin B. The sign flips from minus on the left to plus on the right.

cards.front: Expand tan(A + B).
cards.back: tan(A + B) = (tan A + tan B) / (1 - tan A tan B).

cards.front: Expand tan(A - B).
cards.back: tan(A - B) = (tan A - tan B) / (1 + tan A tan B).

cards.front: Is sin(A + B) the same as sin A + sin B?
cards.back: No. Sine does not distribute over addition. You have to use sin(A + B) = sin A cos B + cos A sin B.

cards.front: How do you check the sign rule for cos(A - B) if you forget it?
cards.back: Set A = B. Then cos 0 = 1, and cos A cos A + sin A sin A = 1. The plus sign is the one that works.

cards.front: Which familiar angles combine to give 75°?
cards.back: 45° + 30° = 75°. That lets you build exact values for 75° out of the 45° and 30° values.

cards.front: Find the exact value of sin 75°.
cards.back: sin(45° + 30°) = sin 45° cos 30° + cos 45° sin 30° = (sqrt(6) + sqrt(2))/4, about 0.966.

cards.front: Find the exact value of cos 75°.
cards.back: cos(45° + 30°) = cos 45° cos 30° - sin 45° sin 30° = (sqrt(6) - sqrt(2))/4, about 0.259.

cards.front: Find the exact value of sin 15°.
cards.back: sin(45° - 30°) = sin 45° cos 30° - cos 45° sin 30° = (sqrt(6) - sqrt(2))/4, about 0.259.

cards.front: Find the exact value of cos 15°.
cards.back: cos(45° - 30°) = cos 45° cos 30° + sin 45° sin 30° = (sqrt(6) + sqrt(2))/4, about 0.966.

cards.front: Find the exact value of tan 75°.
cards.back: tan(45° + 30°) = (1 + sqrt(3)/3) / (1 - sqrt(3)/3), which simplifies to 2 + sqrt(3), about 3.732.

cards.front: Find the exact value of tan 15°.
cards.back: tan(45° - 30°) = (1 - sqrt(3)/3) / (1 + sqrt(3)/3), which simplifies to 2 - sqrt(3), about 0.268.

cards.front: Find the exact value of sin 105°.
cards.back: sin(60° + 45°) = sin 60° cos 45° + cos 60° sin 45° = (sqrt(6) + sqrt(2))/4, about 0.966.

cards.front: Find the exact value of cos 105°.

sets.title: Trigonometry: Double and Half Angle Formulas
sets.description: Double angle formulas for sine, cosine, and tangent, the half angle formulas including all three tangent forms, and the power reduction formulas.

cards.front: State the double angle formula for sine.
cards.back: sin 2θ = 2 sin θ cos θ.

cards.front: State the form of cos 2θ that uses both sine and cosine.
cards.back: cos 2θ = cos²θ - sin²θ.

cards.front: State the form of cos 2θ that uses cosine only.
cards.back: cos 2θ = 2cos²θ - 1.

cards.front: State the form of cos 2θ that uses sine only.
cards.back: cos 2θ = 1 - 2sin²θ.

cards.front: How do you get cos 2θ = 2cos²θ - 1 from cos 2θ = cos²θ - sin²θ?
cards.back: Replace sin²θ with 1 - cos²θ. Then cos²θ - (1 - cos²θ) = 2cos²θ - 1.

cards.front: State the double angle formula for tangent.
cards.back: tan 2θ = 2 tan θ / (1 - tan²θ), valid when tan²θ ≠ 1.

cards.front: State the half angle formula for sine.
cards.back: sin(θ/2) = ± sqrt((1 - cos θ)/2). Choose the sign from the quadrant that θ/2 lands in.

cards.front: State the half angle formula for cosine.
cards.back: cos(θ/2) = ± sqrt((1 + cos θ)/2). Choose the sign from the quadrant that θ/2 lands in.

cards.front: State the square root form of the half angle formula for tangent.
cards.back: tan(θ/2) = ± sqrt((1 - cos θ)/(1 + cos θ)). Choose the sign from the quadrant that θ/2 lands in.

cards.front: State the tangent half angle form with sin θ in the numerator.
cards.back: tan(θ/2) = sin θ / (1 + cos θ). This form carries its own sign, so no sign choice is needed.

cards.front: State the tangent half angle form with sin θ in the denominator.
cards.back: tan(θ/2) = (1 - cos θ) / sin θ. This form carries its own sign, so no sign choice is needed.

cards.front: State the power reduction formula for sin²θ.
cards.back: sin²θ = (1 - cos 2θ)/2.

cards.front: State the power reduction formula for cos²θ.
cards.back: cos²θ = (1 + cos 2θ)/2.

cards.front: State the power reduction formula for tan²θ.
cards.back: tan²θ = (1 - cos 2θ)/(1 + cos 2θ).

cards.front: If sin θ = (3/5) and θ is in Quadrant I, what is sin 2θ?
If sin θ = (3/5) and θ is in Quadrant I, what is cos 2θ?
Use a half angle formula to find cos 22.5°.
cards.back: cos(45°/2) = sqrt((1 + sqrt(2)/2)/2), about 0.924. The sign is positive because 22.5° sits in Quadrant I.

cards.front: Use a half angle formula to find sin 22.5°.
cards.back: sin(45°/2) = sqrt((1 - sqrt(2)/2)/2), about 0.383. The sign is positive because 22.5° sits in Quadrant I.

sets.title: Trigonometry: Law of Sines and Law of Cosines
sets.description: Both laws, which triangle case calls for which, the ambiguous SSA case, and two area formulas for triangles that have no right angle.

cards.front: State the Law of Sines.
cards.back: a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C, where side a is opposite angle A, side b is opposite angle B, and side c is opposite angle C.

cards.front: Which triangle cases call for the Law of Sines?
cards.back: AAS, ASA, and SSA, the cases where you know an angle together with the side opposite it.

cards.front: State the Law of Cosines for side c.
cards.back: c² = a² + b² - 2ab cos C, where C is the angle opposite side c.

cards.front: State the Law of Cosines for sides a and b.
cards.back: a² = b² + c² - 2bc cos A and b² = a² + c² - 2ac cos B. Each angle pairs with the side across from it.

cards.front: Which triangle cases call for the Law of Cosines?
cards.back: SAS and SSS. Neither case hands you an angle paired with its opposite side, so the Law of Sines has nothing to start from.

cards.front: How is the Law of Cosines related to the Pythagorean theorem?
cards.back: When C = 90°, cos C = 0, and the formula collapses to c² = a² + b².

cards.front: How do you solve for an angle using the Law of Cosines?
cards.back: Rearrange to cos C = (a² + b² - c²)/(2ab), then take the inverse cosine of that value.

cards.front: Why is SSA called the ambiguous case?
cards.back: Two sides and a non-included angle can produce no triangle, exactly one triangle, or two different triangles, so you have to test for a second answer.

cards.front: How do you look for the second angle in an ambiguous SSA case?
cards.back: Subtract the first angle from 180°. Keep that second option only if the three angles still total less than 180°.

cards.front: What is the area of a triangle given two sides and the included angle?
cards.back: Area = (1/2)ab sin C, where C is the angle between sides a and b.

cards.front: State Heron's formula.
cards.back: Area = sqrt(s(s - a)(s - b)(s - c)), where s = (a + b + c)/2 is the semiperimeter.

cards.front: When should you reach for Heron's formula?
cards.back: When you know all three sides and no angle. It returns the area without making you find an angle first.

cards.front: What is an oblique triangle?
cards.back: Any triangle with no right angle. Solving one takes the Law of Sines or the Law of Cosines, since SOH CAH TOA does not apply.

cards.front: In a triangle, a = 8, b = 5, and C = 60°. Find side c.
In a triangle, A = 40°, B = 60°, and a = 10. Find side b.
cards.back: b = a sin B / sin A = 10 sin 60° / sin 40°, which is about 13.5.

cards.front: Find the area of a triangle with sides 3, 4, and 5 using Heron's formula.
cards.back: s = 6, so Area = sqrt(6 × 3 × 2 × 1) = sqrt(36) = 6 square units.

cards.front: What is your next step after finding two angles of a triangle?
cards.back: Subtract their sum from 180° to get the third angle, then use the Law of Sines for any side still missing.

sets.title: Trigonometry: Graphs of Sine and Cosine
sets.description: Amplitude, period, phase shift, vertical shift, and midline for y = a sin(b(x - c)) + d, plus where the two parent graphs peak, bottom out, and cross zero.

cards.front: In y = a sin(b(x - c)) + d, what is the amplitude?
cards.back: The amplitude is the absolute value of a, the distance from the midline up to a peak.

cards.front: In y = a sin(b(x - c)) + d, what is the period?
cards.back: 2π divided by the absolute value of b in radians, or 360° divided by the absolute value of b in degrees.

cards.front: In y = a sin(b(x - c)) + d, what is the phase shift?
cards.back: The phase shift is c. Shift the graph right when c is positive and left when c is negative.

cards.front: In y = a sin(b(x - c)) + d, what is the vertical shift?
cards.back: The vertical shift is d. It lifts the graph when d is positive and lowers it when d is negative.

cards.front: In y = a sin(b(x - c)) + d, what is the midline?
cards.back: The horizontal line y = d. The curve rises one amplitude above it and drops one amplitude below it.

cards.front: What does a negative value of a do to the graph of y = a sin x?
cards.back: It reflects the curve across the midline. The amplitude is still the absolute value of a, so only the up and down pattern flips.

cards.front: What is the period of y = sin x and y = cos x?
cards.back: 2π radians, which is 360°.

cards.front: What are the domain and range of y = sin x?
cards.back: Domain: all real numbers. Range: -1 ≤ y ≤ 1.

cards.front: What are the domain and range of y = cos x?
cards.back: Domain: all real numbers. Range: -1 ≤ y ≤ 1.

cards.front: Where does y = sin x reach its maximum between 0 and 2π?
cards.back: At x = π/2, where sin x = 1. In general the peaks sit at x = π/2 + 2πn.

cards.front: Where does y = sin x reach its minimum between 0 and 2π?
cards.back: At x = 3π/2, where sin x = -1. In general the low points sit at x = 3π/2 + 2πn.

cards.front: Where are the zeros of y = sin x?
cards.back: At x = πn for every integer n, so 0, π, 2π, and the same spacing in the negative direction.

cards.front: Where does y = cos x reach its maximum between 0 and 2π?
cards.back: At x = 0 and again at x = 2π, where cos x = 1. In general the peaks sit at x = 2πn.

cards.front: Where does y = cos x reach its minimum between 0 and 2π?
cards.back: At x = π, where cos x = -1. In general the low points sit at x = π + 2πn.

cards.front: Where are the zeros of y = cos x?
cards.back: At x = π/2 + πn for every integer n, so π/2, 3π/2, and the same spacing in both directions.

cards.front: How is the cosine graph a shifted sine graph?
cards.back: cos x = sin(x + π/2). Sliding the sine curve left by π/2 produces the cosine curve.

cards.front: What is the y-intercept of y = a sin(bx)?
cards.back: 0, because sin 0 = 0. The sine curve always starts on its midline.

cards.front: What is the y-intercept of y = a cos(bx)?
cards.back: a, because cos 0 = 1. The cosine curve starts at a peak when a is positive and at a low point when a is negative.

cards.front: Find the amplitude and period of y = 3 sin(2x).
cards.back: Amplitude 3 and period 2π/2 = π.

cards.front: Find the amplitude, period, and midline of y = -2 cos x + 5.
cards.back: Amplitude 2, period 2π, midline y = 5. The negative sign flips the curve, so it starts at a low point of 3.

sets.title: Trigonometry: Graphs of Tangent, Cotangent, Secant, and Cosecant
sets.description: Periods, asymptotes, domains, and ranges for the four reciprocal and quotient graphs, plus how secant and cosecant sit on top of cosine and sine.

cards.front: What is the period of y = tan x?
cards.back: π radians, which is 180°. Tangent repeats twice as often as sine and cosine.

cards.front: What is the period of y = cot x?
cards.back: π radians, which is 180°, the same period as tangent.

cards.front: What is the period of y = sec x and y = csc x?
cards.back: 2π radians, which is 360°. They inherit the period of cosine and sine.

cards.front: Where are the vertical asymptotes of y = tan x?
cards.back: At x = π/2 + πn for every integer n, which is 90° + 180°n. These are the inputs where cos x = 0.

cards.front: Where are the vertical asymptotes of y = cot x?
cards.back: At x = πn for every integer n, which is 180°n. These are the inputs where sin x = 0.

cards.front: Where are the vertical asymptotes of y = sec x?
cards.back: At x = π/2 + πn, the same inputs where cos x = 0, since sec x = 1/cos x.

cards.front: Where are the vertical asymptotes of y = csc x?
cards.back: At x = πn, the same inputs where sin x = 0, since csc x = 1/sin x.

cards.front: What are the domain and range of y = tan x?
cards.back: Domain: all real numbers except x = π/2 + πn. Range: all real numbers.

cards.front: What are the domain and range of y = cot x?
cards.back: Domain: all real numbers except x = πn. Range: all real numbers.

cards.front: What is the domain of y = sec x?
cards.back: All real numbers except x = π/2 + πn, because cos x = 0 at those inputs and sec x = 1/cos x.

cards.front: What is the domain of y = csc x?
cards.back: All real numbers except x = πn, because sin x = 0 at those inputs and csc x = 1/sin x.

cards.front: What is the range of y = sec x?
cards.back: y ≤ -1 or y ≥ 1. Secant never takes a value strictly between -1 and 1.

cards.front: What is the range of y = csc x?
cards.back: y ≤ -1 or y ≥ 1. Cosecant never takes a value strictly between -1 and 1.

cards.front: How does the secant graph relate to the cosine graph?
cards.back: Each secant branch touches a cosine peak or low point at y = 1 or y = -1, then runs off toward infinity at every cosine zero.

cards.front: How does the cosecant graph relate to the sine graph?
cards.back: Each cosecant branch touches a sine peak or low point at y = 1 or y = -1, then runs off toward infinity at every sine zero.

cards.front: Is y = tan x increasing or decreasing between its asymptotes?
cards.back: Increasing. Every branch climbs from large negative values up through 0 to large positive values.

cards.front: Is y = cot x increasing or decreasing between its asymptotes?
cards.back: Decreasing. Every branch falls from large positive values down through 0 to large negative values.

cards.front: What is the period of y = tan(bx)?
cards.back: π divided by the absolute value of b. Tangent uses π in its period formula, not 2π.

cards.front: Where does y = tan x cross the x-axis?
cards.back: At x = πn for every integer n. Those are the zeros of sine, and tan x = sin x / cos x.

sets.title: Trigonometry: Inverse Trig Functions
sets.description: Domains and ranges for all six inverse trig functions, why those ranges are restricted, and how to evaluate compositions such as cos(arcsin x).

cards.front: What are the domain and range of arcsin x?
cards.back: Domain: -1 ≤ x ≤ 1. Range: -π/2 ≤ y ≤ π/2, which is -90° to 90°, covering quadrants IV and I.

cards.front: What are the domain and range of arccos x?
cards.back: Domain: -1 ≤ x ≤ 1. Range: 0 ≤ y ≤ π, which is 0° to 180°, covering quadrants I and II.

cards.front: What are the domain and range of arctan x?
cards.back: Domain: all real numbers. Range: strictly between -π/2 and π/2, that is -90° to 90° with both endpoints excluded.

cards.front: What are the domain and range of arccot x?
cards.back: Domain: all real numbers. Range: strictly between 0 and π, that is 0° to 180° with both endpoints excluded.

cards.front: What are the domain and range of arcsec x?
cards.back: Domain: the absolute value of x is at least 1. Range: 0 ≤ y ≤ π with y ≠ π/2, since sec x is undefined at π/2.

cards.front: What are the domain and range of arccsc x?
cards.back: Domain: the absolute value of x is at least 1. Range: -π/2 ≤ y ≤ π/2 with y ≠ 0, since csc x is undefined at 0.

cards.front: Why are the ranges of the inverse trig functions restricted?
cards.back: The trig functions repeat, so they fail the horizontal line test. Restricting the range picks a single output per input and makes the inverse a true function.

cards.front: How do you write the inverse sine function in symbols?
cards.back: arcsin x, also written as sin raised to the negative one power. That exponent means inverse function, not reciprocal, so it is not 1/sin x.

cards.front: What is arcsin(1/2)?
cards.back: π/6, which is 30°. It is the only angle in the arcsine range whose sine equals (1/2).

cards.front: What is arcsin(-sqrt(3)/2)?
cards.back: -π/3, which is -60°. Negative inputs give negative outputs, since the arcsine range runs from -π/2 to π/2.

cards.front: What is arccos(-1/2)?
cards.back: 2π/3, which is 120°. The arccosine range runs from 0 to π, so a negative input lands in Quadrant II.

cards.front: What is arctan(-1)?
cards.back: -π/4, which is -45°. The arctangent range runs from -π/2 to π/2, so the answer is -45° rather than 135°.

cards.front: Evaluate sin(arcsin 0.4).
cards.back: 0.4. Sine and arcsine undo each other as long as the input sits in -1 ≤ x ≤ 1.

cards.front: Evaluate arcsin(sin 150°).
cards.back: 30°, not 150°. The answer has to land in the arcsine range of -90° to 90°, and sin 150° = sin 30° = (1/2).

cards.front: Why is arccos(cos 300°) equal to 60° and not 300°?
cards.back: The arccosine range is 0° to 180°. Since cos 300° = cos 60° = (1/2), the inverse hands back 60°.

cards.front: Evaluate cos(arcsin(3/5)).
cards.back: (4/5). Draw a right triangle with opposite side 3 and hypotenuse 5, so the adjacent side is 4.

cards.front: Evaluate tan(arccos(5/13)).
cards.back: (12/5). Adjacent side 5 and hypotenuse 13 give an opposite side of 12, so the tangent is 12 ÷ 5.

cards.front: Write cos(arcsin x) as an algebraic expression.
cards.back: sqrt(1 - x²). The arcsine output lies in quadrants IV and I, where cosine is never negative, so the positive root is correct.

sets.title: Trigonometry: Reference Angles and Quadrant Signs
sets.description: What a reference angle is, how to find it in each quadrant, and the ASTC rule for which trig functions come out positive where.

cards.front: What is a reference angle?
cards.back: The acute angle between the terminal side of an angle and the x-axis. It always falls between 0° and 90°, and it is never measured to the y-axis.

cards.front: What is the reference angle formula in Quadrant I?
cards.back: The reference angle is θ itself.

cards.front: What is the reference angle formula in Quadrant II?
cards.back: 180° - θ, which is π - θ in radians.

cards.front: What is the reference angle formula in Quadrant III?
cards.back: θ - 180°, which is θ - π in radians.

cards.front: What is the reference angle formula in Quadrant IV?
cards.back: 360° - θ, which is 2π - θ in radians.

cards.front: What do you do first when finding the reference angle for 500°?
cards.back: Subtract full turns until the angle sits between 0° and 360°. Here 500° - 360° = 140°, in Quadrant II, so the reference angle is 40°.

cards.front: How do you use a reference angle to get an exact trig value?
cards.back: Find the value for the reference angle, then attach the sign the original quadrant requires. Example: cos 150° = -cos 30° = -sqrt(3)/2.

cards.front: What does the mnemonic ASTC, All Students Take Calculus, tell you?
cards.back: Which functions are positive by quadrant: I all, II sine, III tangent, IV cosine. Each listed function also covers its reciprocal.

cards.front: Which trig functions are positive in Quadrant I?
cards.back: All six. Both x and y are positive there, so every ratio comes out positive.

cards.front: Which trig functions are positive in Quadrant II?
cards.back: Sine and cosecant only. There y is positive and x is negative.

cards.front: Which trig functions are positive in Quadrant III?
cards.back: Tangent and cotangent only. Both x and y are negative there, so their quotient is positive.

cards.front: Which trig functions are positive in Quadrant IV?
cards.back: Cosine and secant only. There x is positive and y is negative.

cards.front: On the unit circle, what do the coordinates x and y stand for?
cards.back: x = cos θ and y = sin θ, and tan θ = y/x. The signs of x and y in a quadrant set the signs of every trig value there.

cards.front: Why is tangent positive in Quadrant III?
cards.back: tan θ = y/x, and in Quadrant III both x and y are negative. A negative divided by a negative gives a positive result.

cards.front: Why is cosine negative in Quadrant II?
cards.back: cos θ = x, and every point in Quadrant II has a negative x-coordinate.

cards.front: What is the reference angle for 225°?
cards.back: 45°. The angle is in Quadrant III, and 225° - 180° = 45°.

cards.front: What is the reference angle for 5π/3?
cards.back: π/3. The angle is in Quadrant IV, and 2π - 5π/3 = π/3.

cards.front: What is the reference angle for -120°?
cards.back: 60°. Add 360° to get 240°, which is in Quadrant III, and 240° - 180° = 60°.
